204.title: Al-Buruj: the constellations
204.hook: the people of the ditch who were burned for their faith (85:4–8)
204.howItsDone: Muslims remember the people of the ditch as believers who held firm under persecution; the hadith of the boy and the king is a well-known story told to children and in sermons about steadfastness.

segments.voice: Yesterday: At-Tariq, the night visitor, the piercing star. Your line was every soul has a guardian.

Dubai's skyline has a needle in the middle of it: the Burj Khalifa. Burj means tower. In the plural, buruj, it's the name of the surah before At-Tariq, and there it means the great towers of the night sky: the constellations, the mansions of the stars. The surah opens looking up. But it quickly looks down, into a trench in the ground, at a scene that is hard to hear: people burned for what they believed, while others sat and watched.
screen: `BURJ — A TOWER.` → `BURUJ — THE TOWERS OF THE SKY.` → `A TRENCH IN THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: Surah eighty-five swears by the sky with its constellations, by the promised Day, and by the witness and what is witnessed. Then verse four: destroyed were the people of the ditch, al-ukhdud, the fire full of fuel, as they sat around it, witnessing what they were doing to the believers. Verse eight gives the only charge against the victims: they had nothing against them except that they believed in God, the Mighty, the Praised. The Qur'an doesn't name who they were. The commentators offer two main accounts. One is a long hadith in Muslim's collection about a boy, a king and a monk: the boy's faith spreads to a whole town, and the king has trenches dug and fires lit for anyone who won't turn back. The other, told by Ibn Ishaq and the commentators, connects it to Najran, in southern Arabia, where a king named Dhu Nuwas is reported to have killed the Christians of the town who would not give up their faith. In that reading, the believers the Qur'an honors here were Christians. Either way, the surah doesn't glorify the fire, or ask anyone to seek it. It condemns the people who lit it, and it sees the ones who stood firm. Verse ten leaves a door open: those who persecuted believers, and then did not repent, face the punishment. And then did not repent. Even there, the way back isn't shut. People of many faiths, and none, have been punished for belief, and still are. The surah keeps them in view.

segments.voice: Hold in mind people who are suffering for their beliefs right now, somewhere in the world; no names needed, just a family, a place of worship, a person in a cell. Hold them steadily, the way the surah does, without looking away. If you pray, you can ask for them in your own words.
Al-Buruj. The constellations, the towers of the sky, and the name of Surah eighty-five, which remembers the people of the ditch. Today's word.
Your line: faith under fire. Their only charge was that they believed. Day two hundred four.

205.title: Al-Buruj: the Loving
205.hook: He is the Forgiving, the Loving, Lord of the Throne (85:14–15)
205.howItsDone: Al-Wadud is counted among the ninety-nine names of God; ya Wadud is often said in personal prayer, especially when asking for love and reconciliation between spouses, families and friends.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-Buruj, the constellations, and the people of the ditch. Your line was faith under fire.

A trench, a fire, believers burned, and people sitting around it, watching. What comes after a story like that? Thunder would fit. Something about justice, punishment, the scales set right. And the surah does say, a few verses on, that your Lord's grip is severe. But just after, it names Him with a word that's hard to expect there. A tender word. The word for warm, close affection. Today: al-Wadud, the Loving.
screen: `A TRENCH. A FIRE. WATCHERS.` → `WHAT COMES NEXT?` → `AL-WADUD, THE LOVING.`

segments.voice: Verse twelve: the grip of your Lord is severe. Verse thirteen: He is the one who begins creation and brings it back. And verse fourteen, in Pickthall's words: "And He is the Forgiving, the Loving." Then: Lord of the Throne, the Glorious. Al-Ghafur, the Forgiving, then al-Wadud, the Loving. Wadud comes from wudd, warm affection, the love between people who are close: the hand on the shoulder, the meal saved for you. In Surah nineteen the Qur'an promises that the Merciful will place wudd among those who believe and do good. And it uses al-Wadud as a name of God only twice: here, and in Surah eleven, where the prophet Shu'ayb tells his people: ask forgiveness, turn back, my Lord is Merciful, Loving. Both times it sits next to forgiveness. Some scholars note the form can run two ways: the One who loves, and the One who is loved. God loves His servants, and is loved by them. Now look at where it's placed. Right after the persecutors in the ditch, and right after verse ten, which said the punishment is for those who then did not repent. Forgiving, then Loving. The door left open yesterday has a name on it today. The fire in the trench was real. So is this. Al-Wadud is counted among the ninety-nine names of God, and some call on it when they pray for love between people: between spouses, between families that have drifted, between hearts that have gone cold.

segments.voice: Think of a time love was shown to you: not a feeling, a thing someone did, a meal, a ride at 3am, a note, a hand held in a hospital. Let the memory be clear, and notice that it was love that did something. If you pray, you can say ya Wadud, O Loving One, three times, slowly.

Your line: the loving one. Forgiving first, and then Loving. Two hundred five days in.

206.title: Al-Inshiqaq: the sky splits
206.hook: when the sky splits and the earth stretches, O human, you toil toward your Lord (84:1–6)
206.tomorrow: Al-Inshiqaq: the book in the right hand
206.howItsDone: Al-Inshiqaq contains one of the Qur'an's places of prostration (84:21), where many reciters and listeners bow to the ground; its line 'O human, you are toiling toward your Lord' is often quoted about the dignity of ordinary work.

segments.voice: Yesterday: al-Wadud, the Loving, the name that comes right after the Forgiving. Your line was the loving one.

Look at your hands. Maybe there's a callus from a pen, a keyboard, a steering wheel, a guitar string. A burn from a stove. A scar from a job years ago. Hands keep records of work. Nobody decides to get a callus; it just comes, from doing the same hard thing over and over. The surah just before Al-Buruj opens with the end of the world, the sky splitting open, the earth stretched flat. Then, out of all that, it turns and speaks to you directly, about exactly that kind of work. Today: Al-Inshiqaq, the sky splits.
screen: `A CALLUS, A BURN, A SCAR.` → `HANDS KEEP RECORDS OF WORK.` → `AL-INSHIQAQ, THE SKY SPLITS.`

segments.voice: Surah eighty-four begins: when the sky splits open. Inshiqaq means a splitting, a cracking apart. The sky, the verse says, listens to its Lord and does what it must. Then the earth is stretched out, casts out what's inside it, and is left empty. Everything that seemed permanent obeys and opens. Then verse six turns to the listener: O human being, you are toiling toward your Lord, with real toil, and you will meet Him. The Arabic word is kadih, from kadh. Not light effort: labor that wears you down and leaves marks, like the callus. Classical dictionaries connect it with scratching or scraping, work that leaves a trace on the one doing it. So the surah looks at every human life, the commute, the night shift, the diapers, the exam, the grief, and says: all of that is going somewhere. Then: fa-mulaqih, and you will meet Him. Or, some commentators say, you will meet it: your work, face to face. Both readings are held. Toil here isn't a punishment, and rest isn't wrong. Toil has a direction. You heard it in Al-Layl, efforts differ, and in Al-Ghashiyah, pleased with their effort. Here it's gathered into one sentence: a life's hard work, pointed toward a meeting. This surah also holds one of the verses where many reciters stop and prostrate, a moment built into the Qur'an itself.
screen: `THE SKY SPLITS AND LISTENS.` · `O HUMAN — SPOKEN STRAIGHT TO YOU.` · `KADH — TOIL THAT LEAVES A MARK.` · `YOU WILL MEET HIM, OR IT.` · then, large: `TOILING TOWARD HIM.`

segments.voice: Pick the most tedious task waiting for you, the dishes, the report, the email you've been avoiding, and picture doing it, start to finish. Then see it as part of a long road that's going somewhere, not a pothole in the way. Settle on doing it with care, as if it counts toward a meeting.
Al-Inshiqaq. The splitting, the name of Surah eighty-four: the sky splits, and the human toils toward his Lord. Today's word.
Your line: toiling toward him. Every hard day is on its way somewhere. That's day two hundred six.

207.title: Al-Inshiqaq: the book in the right hand
207.hook: one receives his record in his right hand and returns to his people happy (84:7–9)
207.howItsDone: Muslims believe each person's deeds are recorded and the record is given on the Day of Judgment; many ask God for an easy reckoning and to receive their book in the right hand, and the right hand is used for eating, giving and greeting.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-Inshiqaq, the sky splits, and the human toiling toward his Lord. Your line was toiling toward him.

A name crackles over the loudspeaker at a graduation. A walk across the stage, a diploma placed in a hand, then the turn to scan the crowd. A mother waving. A friend yelling the name too loudly. Then the walk back to them, holding the thing, toward the ones who waited. Al-Inshiqaq shows the end of yesterday's long road as a moment much like this: a record placed in a hand, and a walk back to one's people.
screen: `YOUR NAME IS READ OUT.` → `THE WALK BACK TO YOUR PEOPLE.` → `THE BOOK IN THE RIGHT HAND.`

segments.voice: Verse seven: as for the one given his book in his right hand. The book, kitab, is the record of a life, everything yesterday's toil added up to. Verse eight: he will be reckoned with an easy reckoning. Verse nine: he will go back to his people, rejoicing. Then the other side. Verse ten: the one given his book from behind his back. He'll cry out for ruin. And verse thirteen adds one sharp detail: he used to be happy among his people. Both men are happy among their people, once. One in this life, carelessly. One after the reckoning, with a joy that stays. In Muslim practice the right hand is the hand for good things: eating, giving, greeting. So a record in the right hand is a good record, received with honor. And the easy reckoning? A hadith in Bukhari tells how Aisha, the Prophet's wife, asked about this very verse. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ explained that the easy reckoning is only the presentation: the record is shown, and passed. But whoever is questioned closely, line by line, is in trouble. So the easy reckoning is a kind of mercy, a record glanced at and handed back. Muslims hope for it, and some ask for it by name in their prayers. The surah doesn't say what's in the book. It already said: the toil, and where it was pointed. Today's small deeds are the ink.

segments.voice: Rest your right hand open on your knee, feel its weight, and picture it holding a small book, the record of this one day so far. What's in it? Choose one good deed you could add before tonight, a kindness, a fair word, a debt paid, and close the hand gently around that choice.
Al-Inshiqaq. The splitting, Surah eighty-four, where the book comes in the right hand and its owner goes home rejoicing. Today's word.
Your line: record in the right hand. Both men were happy once; only one joy stayed. Day two hundred seven, done.

208.title: Al-Mutaffifin: short measure
208.hook: woe to those who take full measure and give short (83:1–3)
208.howItsDone: Honest weights and measures belong to Muslim business ethics; Al-Mutaffifin is recalled as a warning against small, hidden cheating, and in the past market inspectors in Muslim cities checked weights and measures.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-Inshiqaq, and the book given in the right hand. Your line was record in the right hand.

You order a large coffee and it arrives two-thirds full. You notice. You pay for a full tank and the pump seems to click off early. You notice that too. Now flip it. The report padded to look finished. The hours logged generously. The split bill where your share gets rounded down. Somehow those are harder to see. It's easy to measure others with a very precise ruler and yourself with a very forgiving one. The surah just before Al-Inshiqaq opens with one word aimed right at that double ruler.
screen: `THE COFFEE, TWO-THIRDS FULL.` → `YOU NOTICE THAT.` → `YOUR OWN, NOT SO MUCH.`

segments.voice: Surah eighty-three begins, in Pickthall's words: Woe unto the defrauders. The Arabic is al-mutaffifin, from tatfif, and commentators tie the word to something small, scant, the scrap left at the bottom. The mutaffif isn't a bank robber. He skims a tiny amount, a pinch off the top, over and over, where nobody can quite prove it. Verses two and three describe him exactly. When people measure for him, he demands it full. When he measures or weighs for them, he gives less. Same scale, two rulers. Then verse four asks: do they not think they'll be raised up, on a tremendous day, the day people stand before the Lord of the worlds? A tiny cheat, set next to the biggest day imaginable. A report in Ibn Majah, from Ibn 'Abbas, says that when the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ came to Medina, its people were among the worst at giving short measure. Then this surah was revealed, and their measuring became good. Whether or not every detail of that report holds, it shows how the first Muslims heard the surah: as marketplace instruction, practical, not abstract. The Qur'an returns to fair measure elsewhere. In Surah Hud, the prophet Shu'ayb tells his people of Madyan: give full measure and full weight, and don't cheat people of what is theirs. Few people weigh grain at a stall anymore. But the measuring hasn't stopped: hours, effort, credit, attention, a fair share of the housework. The market's question still stands. Do you use one ruler for both sides?

segments.voice: Run through the exchanges coming up today, money, work, time, chores, a favor owed, and find one where you might give a little short and take a little full, where nobody would know. Picture giving it full measure instead: the full hour, the fair share, the honest number.
Al-Mutaffifin. Those who give short measure, the ones who skim a little, and the name of Surah eighty-three. Today's word.
Your line: full measure. Even a small pinch, where no one is checking, still counts. See you tomorrow.

209.title: Al-Mutaffifin: the rust on hearts
209.hook: what they earned has rusted over their hearts (83:14)
209.howItsDone: Muslims speak of polishing the heart through tawbah, turning back, and dhikr, remembrance; saying astaghfirullah, I seek God's forgiveness, through the day is one way this is done, recalling the hadith of the black spot that is wiped clean.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-Mutaffifin, and the two rulers, full for me, short for you. Your line was full measure.

Leave a bike out in the rain for one night and nothing happens. Leave it out all winter and you come back to a chain that won't turn. Rust doesn't arrive in a day. It comes a speck at a time, each speck too small to bother with, until the thing doesn't move anymore. Al-Mutaffifin uses that same picture, one anyone who's owned something metal will know, for what a tiny cheat, repeated, does: not to the customer, but to the one doing it.
screen: `ONE NIGHT IN THE RAIN.` → `A WHOLE WINTER.` → `THE RUST ON HEARTS.`

segments.voice: The surah describes people who hear its verses recited and say: stories of the ancients. Old tales, nothing to do with me. Verse fourteen explains why, in Pickthall's words: Nay, but that which they have earned is rust upon their hearts. The Arabic word is rana, a covering, a film, a crust that forms over something and dulls it. It isn't that they can't hear. What they've done has built up, layer on layer, until the heart doesn't catch the light anymore. A hadith in Tirmidhi turns the verse into a picture. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said that when a person does wrong, a black spot is put on the heart. If he stops, asks forgiveness and turns back, the heart is polished clean. If he goes back to it, the spot grows, until it covers the heart. And that, he said, is the rana that God mentions. So the picture has two halves: hearts rust, and hearts shine. Turning back, tawbah, is the polish. So is remembrance of God, which some scholars describe as the heart's cleaning cloth. The man skimming a pinch off every sale doesn't feel like a villain. Each pinch is a speck. But the specks add up, not only in the ledger but in him, until the verses sound like old stories. And a few verses later the surah describes the other record, of the righteous, and says: for this, let those who compete, compete.
screen: `STORIES OF THE ANCIENTS.` · `RANA — A CRUST THAT DULLS.` · `A BLACK SPOT, OR POLISHED CLEAN.` · `LET THOSE WHO COMPETE, COMPETE.` · then, large: `HEARTS RUST; HEARTS SHINE.`

segments.voice: Think of one small habit that's been building up quietly, a little dishonesty, a daily irritation you feed, a thing you keep meaning to stop, and picture it as one spot on something that should shine. Then picture a cloth, and one slow wipe. If you pray, you can say astaghfirullah, I seek God's forgiveness.
Al-Mutaffifin. Those who skim, Surah eighty-three, which says what they earned became rust on their hearts. Today's word.
Your line: hearts rust; hearts shine. In the hadith, the rust can still come off. Day two hundred nine.

210.title: Al-Infitar: the sky cleaves
210.hook: what deceived you about your generous Lord, who made you and shaped you (82:6–8)
210.howItsDone: Al-Infitar is one of the short surahs of the Qur'an's last part; its question, what made you careless of your generous Lord, is quoted as a gentle call to gratitude, and its verses on the noble recording angels shape how Muslims think about their deeds.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-Mutaffifin, and the crust that forms over a heart one speck at a time. Your line was hearts rust; hearts shine.

A hand resting on a table, palm up. Small bones. Tendons that slide like cables. A thumb that can touch every other fingertip, which is how a hand holds a pen, a cup, a baby's head. A hand is so familiar it mostly gets noticed when something goes wrong: a sprain, a cut, a cast. The surah just before Al-Mutaffifin opens with the sky tearing apart, and then, in the middle of that chaos, asks a strangely personal question, about you and the body you're sitting in. Today: Al-Infitar, the sky cleaves.
screen: `A HAND, PALM UP.` → `NOTICED ONLY WHEN IT BREAKS.` → `AL-INFITAR, THE SKY CLEAVES.`

segments.voice: Surah eighty-two begins with four whens. When the sky is cleft apart, infatarat, split like a seam. When the stars are scattered. When the seas are made to burst. When the graves are overturned. Then every soul will know what it sent ahead and what it left behind. Then verse six, in Pickthall's words: "O man! What hath made thee careless concerning thy Lord, the Bountiful, Who created thee, then fashioned, then proportioned thee?" The Lord here is al-Karim, the Generous, the Noble. The question isn't angry. It's almost puzzled. What fooled you? What made you forget the One generous enough to make you? Then three verbs, a craftsman's sequence. Created you. Fashioned you, made you complete. Proportioned you: 'adalak, from the same root as 'adl, justice, balance. Two eyes, two ears, two hands, a body in balance, like a scale set level. Verse eight: in whatever form He willed, He put you together. Look back at the week. Al-Buruj, faith under fire, and al-Wadud, the Loving. Al-Inshiqaq, the sky split and the human toiling toward his Lord, and the record in the right hand. Al-Mutaffifin, full measure and the rust on hearts. Now the sky cleaves again, and between the splitting sky and the recording angels the surah mentions later, it stops to point at something close at hand: a human body, created, fashioned and proportioned, sitting right here.
screen: `FOUR WHENS: SKY, STARS, SEAS, GRAVES.` · `AL-KARIM — THE GENEROUS.` · `CREATED, FASHIONED, PROPORTIONED.` · `'ADALAK — BALANCED, LIKE JUSTICE.` · then, large: `SHAPED IN PROPORTION.`

segments.voice: Hold one hand in the other and feel the bones of the fingers, the soft pad of the palm, the pulse at the wrist; move each finger slowly, and notice how much is working without being asked. Let a word of thanks come, in whatever language you think in. If you pray, you can say alhamdulillah.
Al-Infitar. The cleaving, the sky split open, and the name of Surah eighty-two, which asks what made you careless of your generous Lord. Today's word.
Your line: shaped in proportion. Your hands were made, and balanced. Two hundred ten, and counting.

fork.setup: the sky is cleaving, the stars scatter. then the surah asks you one question. what is it?

how many good deeds did you do?
fork.reveal: What hath made thee careless concerning thy Lord, the Bountiful (82:6): followed by created you, fashioned you, proportioned you.

original.note: Arabic: the Generous, the Noble, a name of God; Pickthall renders it the Bountiful in 82:6.

trapdoor: what you thought: a surah about the sky breaking.
what it means: amid the end of things, a gentle question: what made you forget the generous One who made and balanced you?

what a scholar hears: khalaqa, sawwa, 'adala: create, complete, balance; 87:2 pairs the first two; some early scholars remarked that naming God al-Karim in the question almost suggests its answer: His generosity.
